question: PNP P032 · Products priced above their category average

ctes.required_table:
SELECT
    ProductID,
    Product,
    CategoryID,
    Sale_Price
FROM Products
WHERE CategoryID = 5009
ctes.avg_sale_price:
SELECT
    AVG(Sale_Price) AS category_avg_price
FROM required_table

steps.title: Why does Products supply the rows for this review?
steps.change: Start from 🟦 Products because the report needs one candidate row for each catalogue product. The saved query's first CTE filters that source to Beverages (CategoryID 5009), leaving Tea, Coffee and Juice; Bread is outside the requested category and is removed before the benchmark is calculated.
steps.added_sql:
required_table AS (
    SELECT ProductID, Product, CategoryID, Sale_Price
    FROM Products
    WHERE CategoryID = 5009
)

steps.title: Why does the average CTE return one row?
steps.change: The average is calculated from the three eligible Beverages prices, including products that will not qualify. One row in avg_sale_price represents the single category-wide benchmark (100 + 200 + 300) ÷ 3 = 200.00; it is not one row per product.
steps.added_sql:
avg_sale_price AS (
    SELECT AVG(Sale_Price) AS category_avg_price
    FROM required_table
)

steps.title: Why attach the same benchmark to each product row?
steps.change: The outer query still starts from required_table, so its three rows remain one per Beverages product. The scalar subquery reads the one-row avg_sale_price CTE and repeats 200.0 beside each candidate; no join is needed because the benchmark is a single scalar for the selected category.
steps.sql:
SELECT ProductID, Product, CategoryID, Sale_Price,
       (SELECT category_avg_price FROM avg_sale_price) AS category_avg_price
FROM required_table
ORDER BY ProductID;

steps.title: Why keep only prices above the benchmark?
steps.change: Compare each product's own Sale_Price with the shared benchmark. Tea (100) is below 200, Coffee (200) equals 200 and fails the strict > rule, while Juice (300) is above it and survives. The benchmark is not recalculated from only the surviving product.
steps.sql:
SELECT ProductID, Product, CategoryID, Sale_Price,
       (SELECT category_avg_price FROM avg_sale_price) AS category_avg_price
FROM required_table
WHERE Sale_Price > (SELECT category_avg_price FROM avg_sale_price);

steps.title: Why apply the requested final ordering?
steps.change: The last stage is the exact locked learner query. It keeps the one qualifying product and applies CategoryID ascending, then Sale_Price descending. The result matches the saved expected output.
steps.added_sql: ORDER BY CategoryID ASC, Sale_Price DESC

validation_cases.name: NULL sale price is ignored by AVG and cannot qualify
strict comparison excludes an equal-only category
one product category has no above-average product
